articles.title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
articles.summary: A wrecked air force plane and destroyed buildings are among the images obtained by the BBC's partner CBS News.
articles.body:
Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.

The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings.

The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.

One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public.

"We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face."

The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran.

One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal.

While the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo , apparently of the same radar aircraft in March.

The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats.

At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base.

A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site.

Another image shows a four-storey building damaged by an Iranian strike at Camp Arifjan, in Kuwait.

Damage to the site was reported in March , including on satellite communications hardware, though it is not clear whether this image is from the same attack.

The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict".

It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said.

In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues.

The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions".

A separate report from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7.

The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (£371m), and the estimated total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (£1.4b).

CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports.

Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report.

Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.

Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.

On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval.

The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matte r ahead of the US midterm elections in November.

It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter.

The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US.

The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job".

articles.title: Charlie Kirk's family alleges 'stunning failures' by Utah officials led to his shooting
articles.summary: The conservative activist was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof.
articles.body:
Charlie Kirk's family has accused the Utah Valley University and state officials of "stunning failures and reckless decisions" that they say led to the conservative activist's 2025 assassination during a campus event.

In a legal notice, lawyers for the family say Kirk's Turning Point USA event at the university campus was not properly secured or monitored, making him an easy target.

Kirk, 31, was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus, when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof.

The university said it was aware of the claim but did not comment further on the allegations, according to a statement shared with the BBC's US partner CBS News.

"We are aware of the notice of claim. UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes, " the university said in its statement. "Our focus remains on supporting our campus community."

The legal notice was filed on 9 September, a day ahead of the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, and is typically a precursor to a lawsuit.

It names Utah Valley University, local police, the state of Utah, and other university officials as parties who were allegedly aware of the threats against Kirk and did not take steps to protect him.

"Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie," the notice alleges.

"Placing a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event in the quad surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms is accurately described as walking him into a fishbowl," it says.

Kirk's family alleges the university failed to conduct a meaningful security assessment ahead of the event, failed to assign enough police officers, and did not have an ambulance available on site.

The family also alleges the university ignored warnings about securing the rooftops surrounding the courtyard where Kirk was speaking.

"The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," the family's attorney D Loren Washburn wrote in the court filing.

Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man from Utah, who has been accused of shooting Kirk from a roof, is due to appear in court next month to hear the date of his trial.

Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges.

Prosecutors have called for the death penalty.

articles.title: Sitar, sarod, and shutdown: Curtain falls on a US-India cultural bridge as Kennedy Center shutters
articles.summary: US News: The TOI correspondent from Washington: In an unprecedented crisis for American cultural diplomacy, the board of the Kennedy Center for the Performing .
articles.body: The TOI correspondent from Washington: In an unprecedented crisis for American cultural diplomacy, the board of the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington DC voted on Tuesday to shutter the iconic venue immediately, following a bitter legal battle over President Donald Trump’s demand to add his name to the national memorial. The shutdown, coming after what the administration says is mounting financial strain and structural concerns, puts the future of the country’s premier stage in limbo and delivers a profound blow to global artistic exchanges, including of celebrated artists from India.The board vote came hours after a judge issued a ruling reaffirming that only Congress holds the authority to alter the memorial's name or add new inscriptions to the building. In response, Trump publicly threatened to block a planned multi-million-dollar renovation unless the judicial ruling is overturned, leaving the flagship halls locked indefinitely. A blazing row during the board meeting with Democratic lawmaker Joyce Beatty, during which Trump reportedly called her “dumb” and “obstructionist” and she called him “incompetent” with “more bankruptcies than anyone in the room,” capped the fiasco. “He threw a tantrum.... like an immature child," Beatty said later.Beyond the political fracas, loss of the Kennedy Center reverberates far beyond the Potomac to the banks of the Ganga and Cauvery. For over half a century, the marble institution has functioned as Washington’s window to international masterworks, serving as an essential cultural bridge between East and West. Few artistic traditions reflect this legacy as deeply as the classical and contemporary arts of India.The Center’s Concert Hall and Terrace Theater served as historic showcases for Indian music pioneers. Pandit Ravi Shankar routinely brought his sitar to the venue, delivering transcendent performances of Raga Madhuvanti and Desh that redefined classical music for Western audiences. Tabla virtuoso Ustad Zakir Hussain made the Center a home base for his Masters of Percussion series, weaving intricate rhythmic dialogues that brought packed halls to their feet. In September 2025, sarod grandmaster Ustad Amjad Ali Khan shared the Terrace Theater stage with his sons, Amaan and Ayaan, and young grandsons Abeer and Zohaan, for a rare multi-generational masterclass in lineage and legacy.South Indian traditions shone just as brightly. Legendary vocalist M S Subbulakshmi, Carnatic violin maestro L. Subramaniam, and the late electric mandolin prodigy Mandolin U Srinivas all graced the Center’s acoustic spaces. Langas and Manganiars lit up its Millennium stage. Dance ensembles like Chennai’s Kalakshetra and Bengaluru’s Nrityagram brought the geometry and spiritual depth of Bharatanatyam and Odissi to the 1100-capacity Eisenhower Theater, establishing new standards for Indian choreographic arts in America. “In my experience, Kennedy Center matters as a venue because it commands such a diverse, international audience,” said Anuradha Nehru, an award-winning Kuchipudi artist who is the founder and artistic director of Kalanidhi Dance, which has staged many performances here.Such affection from Indian performers resulted in historic milestones that your correspondent marinated in. Like the 2011 Max India Festival -- a monumental complex-wide takeover featuring over 500 artists across classical music, theater, street performance, and contemporary dance -- as well as landmark tours by cross-genre fusion pioneers Shakti, featuring Zakir Hussain alongside John McLaughlin and Shankar Mahadevan. In 2016, Ranvir Trehan, a leading Indian-American patron of the arts, his wife Adarsh, and their Trehan Foundation, gifted $1 million to the Center to create an India Fund for presenting Indian programming through 2025.For global artists, particularly those from India who spent fifty years building an audience within its grand halls, the curtain falling on the Kennedy Center is more than a local political dispute. It represents an immense loss for international cultural exchange, silencing one of the world's greatest crossroads for artistic dialogue. The current US ambassador to India, Sergio Gor, is on the Board constituted by Trump, but he will be a distant witness to its shuttering.

articles.title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for using ants as garnish
articles.summary: The owner of the acclaimed establishment avoids jail but is made to pay 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965).
articles.body:
A two Michelin-starred restaurant in Seoul has been fined for using ants as a dessert garnish.

The owner of Evett in the South Korean capital was fined 15 million won (£8,144; $10,965), while the company operating the restaurant was fined 10 million won for violating the Food Sanitation Act, local media report.

Ants are not among the 10 insect species approved for human consumption in the east Asian nation. The approved list includes grasshoppers, locusts and some silkworms.

Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the restaurant's owner, as well as a 20 million won fine - but the judge took the owner admitting the charge and having no prior criminal record into account.

However, the judge is reported as saying that, as well as violating food standards, the presence of heavy metals exceeding standards was detected in the ants when they were tested, meaning the "culpability is not light".

The owner was said to have been unaware that providing ants in food was prohibited in South Korea, as they are used as food elsewhere.

Their use as a topping for sorbets at Evett came to light after the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety found online reviews accompanied by photographs.

It said the owner had sprinkled three to five ants on certain dishes to give them a "sour taste", over a period of nearly four years - amounting to approximately 49,000 ants used as a garnish.

Most of the ants were imported from the US, while some came from Thailand, the ministry said.

The owner had argued that they were used in a "small part" of the restaurant's 15-course menu and that diners were told they could opt for a non-ant alternative topping.

Ants are eaten and sometimes even valued as a delicacy in several Asian, African and Latin American cultures. Weaver ants and their eggs are used in Thai and Cambodian cooking, while in Colombia, queen ants are as prized as caviar.

The Michelin Guide considers a two-star establishment as one that does "excellent cooking" and is "worth a detour".

articles.title: In 1877, Frederick Douglass paid $6,700 for a 9.5-acre Washington estate; he turned it into his final home, now a National Historic Site
articles.summary: US News: In 1877, Frederick Douglass bought a hilltop estate in Anacostia, Washington, DC, for $6,700, acquiring a house and roughly over 9 acres of land despi.
articles.body: In 1877, Frederick Douglass bought a hilltop estate in Anacostia, Washington, DC, for $6,700, acquiring a house and roughly over 9 acres of land despite a racial restriction in the property's original deed. Douglass named the estate Cedar Hill and made it his final home. Over the next 17 years, he expanded the house, enlarged the grounds and built a substantial library. Today, the preserved property forms the Frederick Douglass National Historic Site, managed by the National Park Service.Douglass bought Cedar Hill despite a racial covenantDouglass purchased the property on September 1, 1877, from the Freedmen's Savings and Trust Company. The National Park Service records the purchase price as $6,700 for the house and over 9 acres of land. The original deed contained a restriction prohibiting Black people from purchasing the estate, yet Douglass was able to complete the transaction.The property stood on a hill in Anacostia, then a suburban area east of the Anacostia River. Douglass named it Cedar Hill, reflecting the cedar trees growing around the estate. The setting offered him a quieter home away from the more urban surroundings of central Washington.He turned the estate into a much larger homeDouglass did not leave Cedar Hill unchanged. According to the National Park Service, he spent much of his time and money improving the property between 1878 and 1895. He expanded the house from 14 to 21 rooms, added a library and second-storey bedroom, and filled the home with books, art, antiques and other possessions.He also continued acquiring land. In 1878, Douglass purchased some additional acres, bringing the estate to roughly 15 acres. The property was developed with additional structures and cultivated areas, creating what the National Park Service describes as a "gentleman's farm".The library became one of the home's defining spaces. It eventually contained more than 1,000 books covering subjects including history, religion, science and government. Portraits of people Douglass admired, including John Brown, Susan B. Anthony and William Lloyd Garrison, were also displayed there.Cedar Hill remained Douglass's home until his death in 1895Douglass moved into Cedar Hill with his first wife, Anna Murray Douglass, in 1878. He continued living there for the rest of his life, even while his public career took him well beyond Washington. The former abolitionist, author and civil rights advocate later served in several government positions and was appointed US minister to Haiti in 1889.Douglass died at Cedar Hill in 1895, at the age of 77. His connection with the property continued after his death. His second wife, Helen Pitts Douglass, worked to preserve the home. According to The Frederick Douglass Memorial and Historical Association, in 1900 Congress chartered the Frederick Douglass Memorial and Historical Association. Preservation efforts eventually helped keep Cedar Hill available to the public.The home became a National Historic SiteThe National Park Service eventually took responsibility for Cedar Hill, and the property was officially designated the Frederick Douglass National Historic Site. The site preserves the house and landscape associated with Douglass's final years and interprets his life and legacy.Much of the house remains arranged to reflect its appearance during Douglass's lifetime. His roll-top desk remains in the library, while his clothing and Panama hat are among the objects displayed in the home. The National Park Service says the house is furnished with original objects belonging to Douglass and other members of his household.What began in 1877 as a $6,700 purchase of a restricted property became the setting for the final 18 years of Douglass's life. More than a century later, Cedar Hill remains preserved in Washington as a place where visitors can see the home, possessions and landscape connected to one of the most prominent abolitionists and civil rights advocates of 19th-century America. Douglass’ roll-top desk sits in the library, while his Panama hat and clothing are on display in his bedroom. The rooms are also filled with gifts from prominent antislavery figures of Douglass’ time, including President Abraham Lincoln and Harriet Beecher Stow.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Sweden expels Iran embassy employee, citing security concerns
articles.summary: Stockholm says Iran-backed groups are plotting against ‘Jewish and Israeli interests’ in the country.
articles.body:
Sweden has expelled an Iranian embassy employee and summoned the country’s ambassador, accusing Tehran of making threats against Jewish and Israeli interests in Sweden.

Sweden has asked an official at the Iranian embassy in Stockholm to leave the country over activities “not compatible with the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations”, which sets rules for how countries deal with each other’s diplomats.

Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said the decision was taken to protect Swedish citizens and interests, without providing further details.

The country’s Justice Minister Gunnar Strommer later told state broadcaster SVT that the decision involved Iran’s alleged activities against “Jewish and Israeli interests”.

“We know that Iran, over a long period of time, has conducted activities that threaten security in and against Sweden, targeting both individuals who oppose the Iranian regime and various Jewish and Israeli interests in our country,” Strommer said, adding that Iran was “making use of criminal networks” to achieve its objectives.

“We can confirm that Iran continues to engage in activities that pose security threats in and against Sweden. This includes, among other things, attempts to use proxies, such as criminal networks, to carry out attacks or acts of violence,” Jonathan Svensson, spokesman for the Swedish Security Service, told AFP.

In 2024, the service accused Iran of recruiting criminal gang members to commit “acts of violence” against Israeli and other interests in Sweden.

In another incident in 2023, Sweden accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of hacking into a local SMS operator to send 15,000 text messages calling for retaliation after the Quran, Islam’s holy book, was burned during protests.

articles.title: $60 sourdough bread loaf sparks outrage online: 'Would never pay that much'
articles.summary: Martin Auer's New York City bakery sells a $60 rye sourdough loaf made with four organic ingredients and is fermented for 24 hours, sparking debate online.
articles.body: Rye, the first United States location of Austrian bakery Martin Auer, recently opened in New York City — and its $60 loaf of rye sourdough is drawing attention. The new concept on Lafayette Street focuses on one thing: bread. Its 100% rye sourdough is made with "organic Austrian rye flour, water, salt and a lot of time during the process, because it takes a long time to make the bread," co-owner Tim Auer told Fox News Digital. COSTCO SHOPPERS DIVIDED OVER NEW 'SOURDOUGH' BREAD AS CRITICS SAY IT'S NOT THE REAL THING The bakery uses a sourdough culture that Auer said has been in his family for more than 50 years and was brought to New York from Austria. Preparing the sourdough takes about a day, he said. The dough is then mixed, rested, shaped and fermented again before spending about 70 minutes in the oven. After baking, the dense rye loaf needs to rest for at least eight hours before it can be properly sliced. Each full loaf weighs about 3.3 pounds and sells for $60. The $60 price reflects the ingredients and work behind each loaf, as well as the cost of operating in New York, Auer said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The price of the bread is the result of all the efforts and costs that went into this project, but also every single loaf," Auer said. "It's obviously all handmade here on Lafayette Street in one of the most expensive cities in the world, using only the best ingredients, meaning the best rye flour that we import from Austria. And we wanted to give the craft and the bread the stage we think it deserves. And with all these efforts, that's the price." Customers don't have to spend $60 to try it. A half loaf sells for $30 and a quarter loaf for $15, and Rye also sells the bread by the slice. Still, the price has generated criticism on social media. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "I simply would never pay that much for a loaf," one Instagram user declared. Another wrote that "bread is meant to be humble, something you share, not something you flex." "Obviously, $60 is a steep price tag for a single loaf of bread," said Ricky Volpe, a professor of agribusiness at California Polytechnic State University in San Luis Obispo. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS But Volpe said production methods and transportation can contribute to unusually high food prices. "In my mind, it actually would not be crazy as a price if, for example, this was being baked overseas and flown into the United States, because some of the absolute highest-priced food and agricultural items that I can think of rely on air transit," he said. articles.title: How escalating Saudi oil crisis could drive up prices everywhere
articles.summary: BBC Verify's Ben Chu examines what impact rising energy costs could have on the global economy.
articles.body:
Global energy prices have spiked alarmingly again, driven largely in recent days by the escalating conflict between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia causing chaos for the oil industry.

Petrol and diesel costs have risen rapidly in most countries while the wholesale price of natural gas - used for heating homes and generating electricity - has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July.

There are growing concerns of another inflationary shock on the world economy, which could cause interest rates to rise, increase mortgage costs and raise the price of almost everything in the shops including food.

So what is behind this latest surge - and what are the implications for the world economy?

Petrol, diesel and gas prices are rising

The global oil price is currently above $108 (£80) per barrel, up from $70 (£52) in June 2026 - a roughly 50% increase.

This has contributed to average petrol prices in the UK going above 170p a litre, the highest since 2022 and up from 150p in July.

As a result of the near-doubling of UK natural gas costs alongside this the domestic price cap set by energy regulator Ofgem is forecast to rise by 25% in January next year - or about £440 a year for a typical household.

In the US, the cost of a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol has risen from $3.80 (£2.82) in July to $4.32 (£3.20), according to the AAA Gas Prices index.

Diesel prices have hit a record level in the US of more than $6 (£4.46) a gallon, higher even than after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Analysts say the main driver has been a reduction in global oil and gas supplies.

Before the US-Israeli war with Iran began in late February, about 20% of both global oil products and liquefied natural gas supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway connecting the Gulf and the Arabian Sea.

This flow of energy collapsed after February due to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and the energy facilities of US allies in the Gulf as well as a US blockade of Iran's ports.

After the war began, Saudi Arabia stepped up the use of its East-West pipeline - which according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler has a capacity of 3.6 million barrels per day - to export oil via the Red Sea, rather than the Strait of Hormuz.

But the pipeline was forced to shut down after it was attacked by drones on Friday, which Saudi Arabia has blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.

The Houthis separately attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles last week, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted.

Neil Quilliam of Chatham House said the pipeline could be closed for up to eight weeks for repair - although US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told broadcaster CNBC on Tuesday it will start operating again "very soon".

And despite the US government insisting fuel is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz in roughly pre-war volumes, most independent analysts judge that the waterway remains significantly obstructed.

Before the war around 21 million barrels per day of oil and oil products were passing through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

But Kpler estimated this had fallen to about 8.6 million barrels per day by the end of August.

Over the past two weeks, the Houthis in Yemen have captured strategic territory from Saudi-backed pro-government forces close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another trade chokepoint at the southern tip of the Red Sea which was the transit point for about 5% of global oil supplies before February.

About 5% of the global oil supply also normally leaves the Red Sea through the north, via the Suez Canal and a pipeline across Egypt to the Mediterranean.

The global market oil price is rising over concerns these shipping arteries could, like Hormuz, be even more severely disrupted by Iran and its proxies.

Before the Houthis recent advances on the south-west coast of Yemen the group declared in July it was enforcing a naval blockade of Saudi ships and ports. It said it will not attack vessels from other countries passing through the Red Sea.

US President Donald Trump has said "the world's diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran".

Analysts say the conflict - including Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries - has put pressure on diesel prices as Russia is the world's second largest diesel exporter.

But most judge the bigger cause of the recent energy price spike has been the expanding regional conflict in the Middle East.

What does it mean for the global economy?

Economists say that higher global energy prices - if sustained - usually lead to even higher prices for households and weaker economic growth, which translates into lower incomes and wages for people.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has estimated that a sustained 10% increase in oil prices increases global inflation by 0.4% and reduces global GDP growth by up to 0.2%.

The Bank of England has estimated that a 10% increase in global oil price increases the UK inflation rate by 0.5% in the near-term and reduces UK GDP growth by about 0.4%.

The rise in the global oil price since June is about five times larger than in the scenario used by the IMF and the Bank of England in their economic models to assess the impact of rising oil prices.

However, it is possible that the global oil price could drop again if there is a peace agreement between the US and Iran.

After a preliminary deal was signed between the two warring parties in June, the oil price temporarily fell sharply to pre-war levels, having gone as high as $120 a barrel.

articles.title: Ebola fight in DRC ‘far from over,’ warns WHO chief
articles.summary: The DRC faces a growing Ebola threat as cases soar in North Kivu, despite progress in other regions, says Tedros
articles.body:
Despite “encouraging signs” in the fight against the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), efforts to wipe out the virus in the east of the country are “far from over”, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

In an online news conference, WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus told journalists cases were surging in North Kivu province as officials raced to control the spread of “many outbreaks in many places”.

Tedros said the number of weekly cases had doubled over the past two weeks from 100 to more than 200 cases in North Kivu.

“The area is so vast that it’s hard to speak of a single epidemic,” Tedros added.

Tedros said that transmission was declining in the worst-affected areas of Ituri province, the epicentre of the outbreak, while South Kivu has not reported any new cases since May.

“But make no mistake, the epidemic continues to grow and continues to kill”, Tedros warned.

Battling the outbreak has been complicated by the emergence of a rare strain of Ebola known as the Bundibugyo virus, which has no known cure.

WHO said treatment trials and the development of post-exposure prophylaxis were picking up speed.

More than 3,000 healthcare and front-line workers had already been vaccinated with Merck’s Ervebo, said Meg Doherty, WHO’s director of science, research, evidence and quality for health.

Ervebo ⁠is licensed against Zaire ebolavirus, but its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo strain, driving the current outbreak, is ⁠not known.

More than 7,200 cases and more than 3,500 deaths have been reported across seven provinces since the DRC declared its 17th Ebola outbreak in May.

articles.title: In 2025, two boys aged 14 and 12 were dropped at a Michigan man’s home; he kept them together despite no running water and a power cutoff, and strangers have now raised $18,506
articles.summary: US News: Sometimes, a family begins in the most unexpected way. For Sam Restifo, it started in February 2025 when two boys, then 14 and 12, were dropped at his.
articles.body: Sometimes, a family begins in the most unexpected way. For Sam Restifo, it started in February 2025 when two boys, then 14 and 12, were dropped at his home in Saginaw, Michigan, by a woman he barely knew. What followed was not something he had planned for, but he chose to keep the brothers together and care for them when they had few other options, states an online report by 101.3 KFDI. Scroll down to read the inspiring story of existence.A difficult situationThe boys arrived with little family support and a deep fear of being separated if they ended up in the foster care system. Restifo took responsibility for them, but providing a stable home quickly became a struggle, states the news report. The household was without running water, while a power cutoff forced Restifo to depend on a generator for electricity. At the same time, he was trying to navigate the complicated process of getting the boys enrolled in school.Without legal guardianship, even something as basic as registering them for the new school year became difficult. Restifo continued working through the obstacles while trying to make sure the boys had a roof over their heads and remained together.Strangers step inThe family's circumstances gained wider attention after ABC12 reported their story. People who had never met Restifo or the boys began offering financial support.A GoFundMe campaign has since raised $18,506, giving the household some breathing room after months of uncertainty. The money is helping with everyday expenses, household necessities and the costs that come with caring for two growing children. Funds may also go toward legal assistance as Restifo works through the process of seeking guardianship.The support has already begun changing the family's circumstances. Restifo expects the home to have running water and electricity again and is working toward getting the boys back into school. Plans also include buying them new clothes and shoes.Building a future togetherThe unexpected attention has brought another opportunity as well. Restifo's gutter business has received renewed interest, potentially providing another source of income as he works to create greater stability for the household. But the heart of the story remains the relationship that has developed between Restifo and the two boys.What began as an emergency act of kindness has grown into a commitment to keep two vulnerable children together. Now, with financial help arriving from strangers and practical problems beginning to ease, the three are moving toward a future that looks a little less uncertain.For the boys, having someone willing to take them in may have made all the difference. For Restifo, the experience has become a reminder that family is sometimes created simply by refusing to walk away when someone needs you most.Images Courtesy: istock and SunnySkyzCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: A man convicted of providing material support to the Islamic State terror group in connection with the deadly Abbey Gate bombing that killed 13 American service members during the Biden administration's chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan has been sentenced to 20 years in prison. Mohammed Sharifullah, an alleged militant with ISIS-K, a regional branch of the terrorist group, was convicted in April of a conspiracy charge in a deadly 2021 suicide bombing at the Hamid Karzai International Airport in Kabul. During his trial, jurors deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport "resulted from" that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously agreed on that point. AFGHAN MAN CONVICTED OF CONSPIRACY IN DEADLY SUICIDE BOMBING AT KABUL AIRPORT DURING US WITHDRAWAL More than 160 Afghans and 13 U.S. military service members were killed on Aug. 26, 2021, at the airport, where U.S. troops were conducting evacuation operations when a lone suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near Abbey Gate, an entry point. The U.S. withdrawal was completed days later as the Taliban retook control of the country. PENTAGON CRACKS OPEN BIDEN’S BOTCHED AFGHAN WITHDRAWAL AS SWEEPING REPORT READIES ALL THE RECEIPTS During interviews with the FBI, Sharifullah admitted that he surveilled a possible route for the suicide bomber to the Abbey Gate during the last days of the U.S. military’s presence in Afghanistan, according to evidence presented at trial. "ISIS-K members provided Sharifullah with a motorcycle, funds for a cell phone and a SIM card, and instructions to open an account on a particular social media platform to communicate with them during the attack operation," an affidavit cited Sharifullah as saying in an FBI interview. NAVY VETERAN AMONG TRIO WHO ALLEGEDLY WANTED TO BEHEAD SOLDIER AND FUND ISIS DRONE ATTACKS ON AMERICANS "After making these preparations for the attack, Sharifullah was tasked with scouting a route near Hamid Karzai International Airport for an attacker," the affidavit said. "Sharifullah conducted surveillance on a route, specifically checking for law enforcement and American or Taliban checkpoints." Prosecutors also presented evidence of several other ISIS-K attacks in Afghanistan in which Sharifullah admitted involvement. articles.title: Poll shows Americans are increasingly alarmed by AI’s ecological footprint
articles.summary: New poll finds over half of Americans fear AI-driven data centers will hike electricity costs and strain water supplies.
articles.body:
A new survey of adults in the United States finds that more than half worry about artificial intelligence ’s environmental impact, up 12 percentage points from last year.

The poll, a joint effort by The Associated Press, the NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and the University of Chicago’s Energy Policy Institute, indicated that Americans dread AI’s carbon footprint far more than high-emission giants like meat production and aviation.

Released on Wednesday, data from interviews with 3,424 US adults in August show that 53 per cent of Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about artificial intelligence’s environmental impacts. The increased wariness marks an upward trend from the 41 percent recorded last year.

While Democrats are fuelling much of the rise in eco-awareness, with two-thirds expressing great concern compared to half of independents and 4 in 10 Republicans, greater public anxiety is emerging over how local data centres powering AI and cloud computing could affect nearby communities. According to the survey, most Americans are “extremely” or “very” concerned about the impact of data centres on electricity prices or the water supply in the communities where they are built.

“We’re undertaking a massive experiment in real time, and I don’t think there’ll be any putting the milk back in the bottle,” said Michael Greenstone, who directs the University of Chicago institute that collaborated on the survey. “Change is scary, and I think some of that is being reflected here.”

Despite bipartisan pushback , thousands of data centres already span the US, with extensive construction underway to meet escalating demand. The scope includes decades-old conventional facilities alongside massive and newly built hyperscale centres engineered for resource-intensive AI processing. While Virginia and Texas lead the nation in operating facilities, California, Ohio and New York follow behind closely as top digital infrastructure hubs.

United States President Donald Trump has urged communities across the country to embrace the tech facilities, promising that they will bring jobs.

“There’s a lot of water usage by AI data centres that’s taking away from other things like agriculture and farmers and places that really need it, and people who really need it,” Gedeon Kebede, a computer science student and Democrat from Cincinnati, Ohio, told the AP.

While data centres aren’t the US’s largest water gobblers, they still retain water to cool AI chips and computers and can be “nationally modest but potentially locally decisive”, according to Fengqi You, an energy systems professor with Cornell University.

“I think that decisions are being made for the company, not for the community that they’re being built in,” Nancy Antunes, a 60-year-old retired Democrat from Waltham, Massachusetts, told the AP.

articles.title: Body found in search for missing Suffolk boy Noah Woods, 3
articles.summary: About 1,300 volunteers joined police in searching for Noah, who went missing from a playground.
articles.body:
A body has been found in the search for missing three-year-old boy Noah Woods, police have confirmed.

Noah disappeared at about 15:00 BST on Tuesday from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk.

Supt Tom Pearse of Suffolk Police said dive teams recovered the body of a child from a nearby pond.

He said the death was being treated as unexplained but not suspicious.

Supt Pearse said formal identification had yet to take place, but Noah's family had been informed.

"Our thoughts are with Noah's family and all those who knew him," he said.

"We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help."

Police said at least 1,300 members of the public had helped in the search for the missing boy, who was non-verbal and partially deaf.

People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire had turned up to help.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the estuary of the River Stour on the Essex border.

Volunteer efforts had been co-ordinated from Brantham Leisure Centre and the village hall, which ran out of hi-vis vests due to the number of volunteers.

Those looking for Noah had been told he would not respond to shouting.

Searches had widened to include East Bergholt and Manningtree, over the Essex border, on Wednesday.

Divers from the Metropolitan Police were called in to search Decoy Pond, a nearby fishing lake.

The pond is about 350 yds (320m) away from the playground where Noah was last seen.

Supt Pearse continued: "Since Noah was reported as missing, a vast number of our officers and staff have been deployed in numerous functions in the search for Noah and support for his family.

"We've been supported by Suffolk HART (Hazardous Area Response Team), SULSAR (Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue), Environment Agency, HM Coastguard, Fire and Rescue Service and the ambulance service.

"As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community and the heart-warming nature of Suffolk people that make the county such a special place.

"I am sure you appreciate the family now need time, space and privacy and I thank you for your understanding in this."

articles.title: UN chief warns AI race could trigger ‘gigantic disaster’ as Trump rejects tighter controls
articles.summary: Rest of World News: UN secretary general Antonio Guterres has warned that the rapid advance of artificial intelligence cannot be allowed to outpace safeguards, calling fo.
articles.body: UN secretary general Antonio Guterres has warned that the rapid advance of artificial intelligence cannot be allowed to outpace safeguards, calling for stronger international oversight.The warning comes as US president Donald Trump argues that the United States already has sufficient protections in place and has dismissed calls from technology executives for tighter controls on AI.Speaking ahead of next week’s UN General Assembly in New York, Guterres said governments had a responsibility to address concerns raised by those developing the technology.“We cannot afford to ignore concerns that have been raised, especially by those on the front lines of the development of AI,” Guterres said. “It’s the first responsibility of any government to protect its citizens – including from the threats of artificial intelligence.”Guterres said countries leading the development of frontier AI should establish “mechanisms of contact, of exchange of information and some common guardrails” to prevent what he called a “race to the bottom”.He warned that such a race “could lead one day to a gigantic disaster at the global level”.The UN Security Council may also discuss AI next week during the annual gathering of world leaders, diplomats said. The 15-member council first held a meeting on artificial intelligence in 2023.The warning comes days after Trump rejected calls from technology executives for tighter oversight and a slower pace of AI development. On Monday, Trump said the US already had the regulatory and criminal powers needed to deal with AI companies.“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. He also described concerns over AI and data centres as a “SICK conspiracy”.The dispute follows warnings from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who has called for independent audits of the most advanced “frontier” AI models. His proposal received backing from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk of xAI.Public concern has also intensified after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said he resigned partly because “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.Guterres said the priority should be a shared framework for the technology. “We need a shared understanding of how to advance the safe, secure and responsible development of AI,” he said, while identifying when increasingly powerful systems may require “stronger safeguards” or additional measures.Additionally, Guterres called for accountability for countries supplying weapons to Sudan’s warring parties when those arms are used against civilians.Describing the humanitarian crisis as “devastating” and the suffering as “intolerable”, Guterres said the conflict is being fuelled by external actors. Sudan’s war, which began in April 2023, has displaced more than 14 million people.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: NBC Los Angeles helicopter crash shatters tight-knit local news community
articles.summary: The television news helicopters that circle Los Angeles have been fixtures of the city’s sky for decades, symbols of a hard-driving but close-knit media market.
articles.body: The television news helicopters that circle Los Angeles have been fixtures of the city’s sky for decades, symbols of a hard-driving but close-knit media market. The crews aboard the choppers cover police chases and FBI raids, Hollywood scandals and sports celebrations, earthquakes and wildfires. The city’s TV news community was confronted with a tragedy of its own Tuesday when a helicopter used by the local NBC station crashed and burst into flames while hovering near the scene of a fatal bus collision. The chopper crash killed the two people aboard, journalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw, and one person on the ground. Two people died in the bus collision. In wrenching on-air remarks and social media posts, Los Angeles news anchors and their colleagues attempted to process their grief while continuing to report on the accident. The outpouring illustrated the tight bonds linking colleagues who found themselves at the center of the story in the nation’s second-largest broadcasting center. NBC Los Angeles’ Robert Kovacik, who joined the station 22 years ago, reported live from a commercial intersection in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in the San Fernando Valley. Microphone in hand, he stood just feet away from the Metro bus and the SUV that had collided when his crew’s cameras panned to plumes of black smoke rising behind a nearby 7-Eleven. He rushed to that scene. Colleen Williams, a 40-year veteran of NBC Los Angeles and one of the city’s most recognizable broadcasting personalities, confirmed on air hours later that the station’s helicopter had gone down. Hands clasped, she spoke haltingly and seemed to fight back tears. “We’ve been piecing it together here. We knew it was a news chopper, we knew we’d lost contact with our people out there, and we’ve just received the confirmation that, in fact, NewsChopper4 went down just before 7 o’clock tonight in Chatsworth,” Williams said to the camera. “We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, to process and to regroup.” Kovacik sobbed and wiped away tears from inside a Los Angeles Police Department vehicle. He kneeled behind yellow police tape as elected officials, including Mayor Karen Bass, held an evening news conference about the accidents. “This is a very, very, very tragic day in Los Angeles,” Bass said. The news conference was short and solemn. Reporters from other outlets remained mostly silent, asking the mayor only one question. In tragic moments like these, Bass said, Los Angeles residents do what they do best — “come together.” When the news conference concluded, Bass approached Kovacik and gave him a long hug. Political officials and first responders expressed their condolences to him; Kovacik thanked firefighters for arriving so quickly and doing everything they could to help Moreno and Marciniw. The cause of the crash remained unknown Wednesday. Jeff Wald, a former news director at rival local station KTLA, said Tuesday’s accidents were so devastating for the city partly because of the familial atmosphere inside the walls of its local newsrooms. “What happens in this business is you wind up spending holidays, weekends, late nights and early mornings with these people, your colleagues. They become your second family,” he said in a phone interview. “Whenever I would hire somebody for these types of helicopter jobs, I worried about their safety.” In a post on X, Frank Buckley, an anchor at KTLA, paid tribute to “our friends at NBCLA on a painful evening.” “The helicopter pilots and crews at all of our stations are vital members of our teams who are dedicated to informing the public and this is a terrible loss,” he wrote. Elex Michaelson, a CNN anchor who formerly co-hosted the evening news broadcast on KTTV, the local Fox affiliate, wrote on X that helicopters are “essential to covering the biggest stories in the vast news market of Southern California.” (In fact, news helicopters were pioneered in Los Angeles in the late 1950s.) “I interned at NBC4 for years in college. Their team is filled with extraordinary people and great journalists,” Michaelson wrote in part. “My heart breaks for their team and the loved ones of everyone who lost their lives.” Tuesday’s chopper accident took place 49 years after a Bell 206 news helicopter piloted by KNBC’s Francis Gary Powers, a former U.S. Air Force officer and CIA employee, crashed near the Encino neighborhood, killing him and cameraman George Spears. The two were returning from covering wildfire in Santa Barbara when their chopper lost fuel and came down. Desmond Shaw, a helicopter news reporter for the CBS LA station, appeared Tuesday night from the seat of his chopper. He reflected on recent losses in his personal life, including the deaths of his parents, and said that anguish was “compounded” by news that the city itself had been struck by “a double tragedy.” “The poor people that were caught in that bus crash today, I don’t want them to be forgotten either,” he said. Shaw then invoked one of the core tenets of the news profession. “We’re always saying, out of safety: cover the news, don’t be the news,” he said. “Unfortunately, gut-wrenchingly, they were part of the news tonight.”

articles.title: South Africa slams planned US sanctions over alleged racial discrimination
articles.summary: Trump administration falling for misinformation from ‘fringe groups’ alleging discrimination against white Afrikaners.
articles.body:
South Africa has called the United States’s plans to impose sanctions on individuals there for alleged discrimination against white Afrikaners a result of “mischaracterisations” being promoted by “fringe groups”.

“We remain committed to addressing these challenges through our constitutional institutions, democratic processes and the rule of law, with the objective of building a more equal and inclusive society for all South Africans,” South African Minister for International Relations and Cooperation Ronald Lamola said in a statement on Wednesday.

Lamola was responding to an announcement made on Tuesday by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio that Washington would be enacting a new policy aimed at South Africans involved in what he called “race-based” discrimination against white Afrikaners.

Rubio said the US would restrict visas for individuals “responsible for, or complicit in the enactment or implementation of laws or policies that enable uncompensated land seizures, race-based discrimination, and/or the incitement of imminent violence against members of minority ethnic or racial groups in South Africa”.

Afrikaners are a minority in South Africa that descends from mostly Dutch colonial settlers, who formalised a system of apartheid in the country that saw land and resources seized from the majority Black population, who were largely relegated to live in enclaves called “Bantustans”.

The apartheid system persisted until 1994, when the country’s first democratic elections brought Black Africans into power.

A 2017 South African government report found that whites, who make up about 7 percent of the population, owned disproportionately large amounts of land, including 72 percent of the individually owned farmland.

South Africa has undertaken programmes to buy land and redistribute it, and in 2025 passed a law that would allow expropriation of land, including in some limited cases without compensating owners.

US President Trump has been lobbied by Afrikaner groups decrying that law and what they say is government-backed discrimination and violent attacks against them, claims that the South African government says are misinformation.

South Africa has also been targeted by Trump for its filing of a case in the International Court of Justice accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.

The Trump administration has allowed white Afrikaners to receive asylum in the US, and last year froze most foreign assistance to South Africa.

articles.title: Steel Across America ends its cross-country 9/11 memorial at NY Giants game
articles.summary: Tunnel to Towers' Steel Across America tour carried a 16,900-pound South Tower beam across 38 stops before its emotional finale at MetLife Stadium.
articles.body: The Tunnel to Towers Steel Across America tour concluded its more than 38 stops with a final appearance at MetLife Stadium for a New York Giants game this week. The tour featured a 21-foot steel beam from the South Tower of the World Trade Center. Starting in May, the tour traveled from the East Coast across the U.S. and then went to the New York City area to mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11 before Sunday's last stop. The 16,900-pound piece of steel – recovered from Ground Zero in the days after the attacks by first responders who rushed to the site – has since become a symbol of the nearly 3,000 civilians, firefighters, police officers, emergency workers and military personnel who died that day. GIANTS HONOR 9/11 HEROES BEFORE EMOTIONAL SUNDAY NIGHT FOOTBALL OPENER AGAINST COWBOYS "For the past four months, communities across the country have welcomed this sacred piece of American history with incredible emotion," Tunnel to Towers Chairman and CEO Frank Siller said in a press release. "Watching people stand in front of that steel, hugging it, praying over it, weeping, reminds me every single day of why we do this work." ‘THEIR SOULS ARE IN THAT STEEL’: 9/11 BEAM MAKES EMOTIONAL STOP IN INDIANAPOLIS BEFORE RETURN TO NYC An August ceremony in Indianapolis included a color guard, a pipes and drums procession, the national anthem performed by the Voices of the Indianapolis Fire Department and an invocation from Indianapolis Fire Department Chaplain Mike Gatliff. Indianapolis Fire Division Chief Tom Neal and Timothy Winslow, a retired major general and executive director of the Indiana War Memorial and Museum, also addressed the crowd about the connection between the city’s first responders, veterans and the legacy of 9/11. 9/11 SENT THEM TO WAR. 25 YEARS LATER, VETERANS GRAPPLE WITH WHAT FOLLOWED "Bringing this steel to Indianapolis, and to a museum that has stood for over a century as a tribute to American sacrifice, is deeply moving," FDNY Lt. Jack Kielty, a Tunnel to Towers board member, said. "Indiana veterans and first responders understand what it means to serve." The event also highlighted Indiana’s own connection to the attacks. Nine Hoosiers died on Sept. 11, while Indianapolis Task Force One sent rescuers to Ground Zero. Six members of the team later died from illnesses linked to their work in the toxic environment, according to the Indiana War Memorial. Scott Nokes, a Marine Corps veteran and Tunnel to Towers recipient, spoke to attendees about the significance of allowing people to see the steel in person. "Out of the 2,977 lives that were lost, there’s over 1,000 bodies that were never recovered specifically from Ground Zero in New York," Nokes said. "Their souls are in that steel, and if you touch it, you feel it." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP On the 25th anniversary of 9/11, Frank Siller and his family honored his late brother Stephen Siller — a heroic 34-year-old husband, father and firefighter who, after hearing about the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attack, loaded himself down with gear, and traversed through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel on foot heading to the Twin Towers, and ultimately giving his life — by retracing the man's steps. "This morning’s walk through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel was part of the conclusion of Steel Across America, a journey that began four-and-a-half months ago and carried a 21-foot, 16,900-pound World Trade Center steel beam more than 10,500 miles through nearly 40 stops across the country and back, stopping in more than 21 states," a statement from Tunnel to Towers said. "For over four months, the steel has been a gathering place for communities to remember the events of September 11th, to honor first responders and veterans, and to ensure that a new generation understands the significance of what happened 25 years ago."

articles.title: Fellow vet remembers late Army paratrooper who helped Fox News reporter, Afghans and Helene victims: 'Send me'
articles.summary: Army veteran Sean Michael Lee served with the 82nd Airborne Division and later helped evacuate allies from Afghanistan and set up aid stations in Poland.
articles.body: Sean Michael Lee dedicated his life to serving others. The Army veteran with more than 20 years of military experience spanning multiple deployments and companies — including as a paratrooper for the vaunted 82nd Airborne Division — did not retire his commitment to help others when he finished his military career. "His entire life was in service to others. Up until the very end, Sean was always thinking of others," Steven Rozina told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. Rozina, now the deputy chief operating officer for the nonprofit Independence Fund, which helps provide services and support to wounded veterans, met Lee when he too joined the nonprofit to continue his career of service. ARMY VETERAN PARATROOPER WHO DEPLOYED TO IRAQ, AFGHANISTAN BEFORE HELPING RESCUE FOX NEWS REPORTER DEAD AT 50 "He immediately took me under his wing as somebody to teach you how to help others," Rozina told Fox News Digital. Rozina outlined Lee’s impressive post-military resume, which spanned three continents, in his efforts to continue helping people. "I think it was 2021, the fall of Afghanistan. Sean answered that call again. He helped evacuate thousands of our Afghan allies, people that worked with us, people that are our friends, that are still our friends today," Rozina explained. MCCHRYSTAL, BRIDGELAND: WANT TO STRENGTHEN AMERICA? REQUIRE A YEAR OF NATIONAL SERVICE "He got done with that mission and Sean answered the call again. When Russia invaded Ukraine, he went to Poland," Rozina said. "He helped set up aid stations, helped set supply lines. And even when a Fox News reporter, Benjamin Hall, was injured and was essentially lost, Sean was that guy that helped organize the efforts to bring Benjamin home. Sean was never the guy on the front page of the paper, but he was always there." Coordinating a rescue operation from Poland via another nonprofit group, Save Our Allies, Lee was instrumental in the efforts to bring Hall home after a Russian attack badly wounded him while he was reporting on the war near Kyiv. AMERICA'S WOUNDED, STRUGGLING VETERANS GET BRAND-NEW HOMES BUILT BY FLORIDA TEENS In 2024, Lee again jumped into action when Hurricane Helene devastated parts of the Southeast, including his home state of North Carolina — particularly its western mountains. "Within a few hours, Sean was in the car, and he was headed up to the mountains," Rozina told Fox News Digital. 9/11 HERO’S MEMORY PRESERVED THROUGH MASSIVE EFFORT TO ‘DO GOOD’ FOR VETS, FIRST RESPONDERS: ‘HIS LEGACY’ "I spent a lot of time with Sean up in the mountains. I got the call, and he needed me to come with him, and we slept in our cars and helped set up aid for different communities," Rozina continued. However, Rozina explained, "when many of us went home, Sean stayed." "Sean stayed in the mountains, he lived in tents, stayed with communities that didn't have a lot, helped rebuild family homes, helped rebuild… there was a family store that, it was the only thing that these people had, and he was there, he was always there for somebody else," Rozina explained. AMERICA'S WOUNDED COPS FIND HOPE, HEALING AND SECOND CHANCE THROUGH OFFICERS WHO REFUSE TO LEAVE THEM BEHIND Lee died Tuesday as a result of cancer he developed from exposure to toxic burn pits during his time deployed in the Middle East. He was still working out how to keep helping people until the very end of his life, Rozina said. "I have a text message from last week where he's making plans for the next mission. The next thing that he wanted to do to make sure if another hurricane hits North Carolina, how are we going to respond? If an earthquake happens, where are we gonna go and how can we be more efficient? How can we help more people?" Rozina told Fox News Digital. VETERANS FACE SURPRISING THREAT AFTER CANCER DIAGNOSIS, STUDY REVEALS "Sean, in his own words, was a good 'idea fairy.' Sean came up with great ideas and really it was... Sean's plans were to be prepared, always be prepared. And it was ideas on how can we be prepared for the next emergency; the next time a veteran needs us, how can [we] incorporate our veteran community into helping others? And that was his goal was really to spread who he was, that 'send me' ethos," Rozina said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Lee's work, through the Independence Fund and through Save Our Allies, was about helping people and using his own gifts and talents to do so, Rozina explained. When asked what he thought Sean's final message to the world would be, he said, "Any help is still help.""You might feel like you're not doing much, but doing something means a lot. So, do what you can," Rozina said of his late friend. "Do the best you can when you're doing it. And do it with a grateful heart. What Sean did: He did the best he could at everything. And those little things add up in the end. He's touched so many lives. He has blessed a lot of deserving people and I know that his memory is not going to fade."

articles.title: Belarus frees 25 political prisoners in return for US sanctions relief
articles.summary: The Trump administration said more releases would be secured soon amid improved US-Belarus relations.
articles.body:
Belarus on Wednesday freed 25 political prisoners as the United States lifted sanctions on two of the reclusive country’s companies, US envoy John Coale announced after his latest visit to Minsk.

The release on Wednesday marked the culmination of a series of negotiations stretching back more than a year between Coale and Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Those freed include human rights campaigners, political activists, journalists and lawyers.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius, where the freed prisoners were taken, Coale said he expected to return in about a month when he hopes to see “hundreds” freed.

The US envoy praised US President Donald Trump on social media, saying his “commitment to direct diplomacy delivers results” and that the administration would continue to “improve US-Belarus relations”.

Coale had been tasked by Trump with securing the release of hundreds of people. In March, the government of Belarus released 250 prisoners following a pardon.

Lukashenko, in charge of the former Soviet state since 1994, has long been shunned by the West for repressing his opponents and supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine .

The releases came a day after Coale promised Lukashenko that US banks would return tens of millions of dollars in ⁠frozen Belarusian assets.

The US envoy earlier said that the US would lift sanctions on Lakokraska, a paint and industrial coating manufacturer, and Bellesbumprom, a state-owned industrial enterprise that oversees the forestry, pulp and paper sectors.

Christian Wigand, the European Union’s lead spokesperson for foreign affairs and security policy, said the 25 prisoners were released as a result of US efforts.

“We welcome this step,” he wrote on X. “800+ individuals remain arbitrarily detained in appalling conditions. Belarus’ regime should release all political prisoners, immediately and unconditionally.”

Journalists, musicians among those arrested

The Belarusian human rights watchdog Viasna, which the government banned after declaring the group an extremist organisation, said many of those released on Wednesday had been sentenced to several years in prison.

The organisation named journalist Andrei Alyaksandrau, who had been serving a 14-year term, among those released. Alyaksandrau had been arrested in 2021 for allegedly “financing protest activities” alongside his girlfriend Iryna Zlobina, who was handed a nine-year sentence.

Alyaksandrau told Viasna he had lost 30kgs (66 pounds) while in captivity “for the motherland” but was “in a good mood”. He added that he was “very glad that these almost six years are over” and that he hadn’t seen Zlobina – whom he married in a pre-trial detention centre in 2022 – in four years.

Alongside Alyaksandrau, three other journalists – Dzmitry Navazhylau, Kiryl Pazniak and Liudmila Chekina – were released and immediately deported to Lithuania. Reporters Without Borders said it was “delighted” by their release but denounced their expulsion.

Exiled political opposition leader Svetlana Tsikhanouskaya said she was happy for the relatives of the 25 freed prisoners “who have been waiting for this day”. Her husband, Siarhei Tsikhanouski, was freed last year after spending five years in jail.

“Every release requires tremendous effort, and it is clear that [Lukashenko] does not want to release all political prisoners,” she wrote on X, noting that hundreds more remain behind bars.

articles.title: Meet Joey: The 2-year-old Los Angeles rescue dog credited with finding 3 people alive beneath earthquake rubble is now up for a national hero award
articles.summary: US News: When disaster strikes, concrete dust and debris cover everything in sight, and finding someone alive can seem an almost impossible task. That impossib.
articles.body: When disaster strikes, concrete dust and debris cover everything in sight, and finding someone alive can seem an almost impossible task. That impossible task is what Joey, a 2-year-old Labrador Retriever with a nose for the impossible and months of specialized training, was trained to do.The Los Angeles County Fire Department’s search-and-rescue K-9 has already proven himself a valuable addition to the team, helping to find three people alive in earthquake debris. Now the young dog is receiving national recognition as a semifinalist in the American Humane Society’s 16th annual Hero Dog Awards, states an online report by abc7.From practice to realityAccording to the report, Joey is employed by the Urban Search and Rescue Task Force, USA-2, Los Angeles County Fire Department. He and his handler, Los Angeles County Fire Capt. Louis Gudiel, trained together for more than five months before passing their certification in September 2025. The tough training made the duo mission-ready for deployments wherever their skills were required. For Joey, it meant learning to search unstable disaster sites and to detect people who might be buried in the rubble of collapsed structures. His first big overseas deployment came in June, when he and Gudiel went to Venezuela in the wake of a deadly earthquake.Three lives discovered under rubbleThe team arrived three days after the earthquake, when hopes of finding survivors were already racing against the clock. Joey went to work on the rubble, using his highly developed detection abilities to search areas where people could be trapped and difficult to reach. He found three survivors alive under the rubble during the mission, informs the online report.The discovery underlined the importance of specially trained K-9 teams in the event of major disasters. Dogs like Joey can search big, dangerous areas much faster and more effectively than human rescuers working by themselves, giving trapped victims a vital chance of being found.Hero even off dutyJoey’s work doesn’t stop once the rescue gear is off. The Labrador is now back at his station in Los Angeles, where he provides comfort to firefighters and other first responders. Off the rubble, Joey is much like any other young dog. He shows a softer side to the K-9 who has worked in some of the roughest conditions in the world, enjoying playing his ball at the park and spending time with his family.Now, his rescue work has landed him a spot as a semifinalist for the Hero Dog Awards, drawing national attention to a young Labrador whose nose, training, and determination have already saved lives.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Attorneys in Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs’ $100M defamation lawsuit seek to withdraw over months of unpaid fees
articles.summary: Attorneys for Sean “Diddy” Combs’ are dropping the rapper and music executive as a client in his $100 million defamation lawsuit.
articles.body: Attorneys for Sean “Diddy” Combs’ are dropping the rapper and music executive as a client in his $100 million defamation lawsuit. Michael Tremonte, a partner at Sher Tremonte LLP, said Combs, 56, “has not paid a substantial balance of attorney’s fees, costs, and expenses,” according to a declaration to withdraw as counsel, filed Monday in the Southern District of New York. Tremonte said in the filing that Combs is more than six months behind on fees, and that there has been “a total breakdown in cooperation and communication between Mr. Combs and the Firm.” Combs has “declined to make himself available for timely, substantive, and direct communications about his cases for over four months,” the filing states. “The Firm’s representation has been rendered unreasonably difficult by Mr. Combs’s lack of cooperation, resulting in a breakdown in attorney-client communications and rendering Sher Tremonte incapable of continuing to provide effective legal services to Mr. Combs,” the filing says. Tremonte was defending Combs in civil litigation, including a $100 million defamation lawsuit against Courtney Burgess, Ariel Mitchell and Nexstar Media Inc. He did not represent Combs in his criminal trial in New York City last year. Through his spokesperson, Juda Engelmayer, Combs said the split was his decision. “I made the decision to switch lawyers because I won’t let anyone take advantage of me by overcharging me and running up bills that were never approved,” he said. “This is strictly a business matter, and any talk about unpaid fees is just part of our dispute over those unapproved charges.” Tremonte pushed back in an email, writing that his firm “represented Mr. Combs zealously and very efficiently under challenging circumstances.” “As stated in our court filings, we are withdrawing from representing him because he has not paid his long-overdue invoices and has become uncooperative,” Tremonte said. “Any suggestion that we overcharged him is simply false.” Combs is serving a 50-month sentence at a New Jersey federal prison on two interstate prostitution convictions stemming from that case. Prosecutors had sought 11 years. He was acquitted of the more serious charges, including racketeering and sex trafficking and has maintained his innocence, pleading not guilty to all counts. His release is scheduled for May 8, 2028, according to Federal Bureau of Prisons records, thought it could come sooner with good behavior. In July, Combs was moved to solitary confinement after a fight with another inmate, a source with knowledge of the matter told NBC News.

articles.title: UK trade unions back motion to boycott and sanction Israel
articles.summary: Motion demands taking action to oppose the ‘catastrophic destruction of Gaza’ and Israeli settler violence.
articles.body:
The umbrella organisation for trade unions in the United Kingdom has passed a motion calling for an end to complicity in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and settler violence in the occupied West Bank.

The Trades Union Congress, representing more than 5.3 million workers, voted in favour of the motion on Wednesday during its annual conference in Brighton, southern England. The vote marks the first time the congress has backed the Palestinian-led movement Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions known as BDS .

“It’s essential for the trade union movement to answer the call from the BDS movement, to challenge all complicity and to use our collective powers, to stand shoulder to shoulder with Palestinians to Free Palestine,” said Zita Holborne from Artists’ Union England, which put forward the motion.

The unanimous vote demands that the Trades Union Congress take action to oppose what the motion described as the “catastrophic destruction of Gaza” and Israeli settler violence “supported by the IDF [Israeli army]”.

The steps include campaigning to end military cooperation and arms deals with Israel, calling on the government to impose wide-ranging sanctions on Israel and backing trade union-led campaigns in support of Palestine.

Co-founder of the BDS movement, Omar Barghouti, welcomed the development.

“This mass movement of solidarity with the people of Palestine, led by Palestine Solidarity Campaign with many trade unions affiliated to it, is the reason why your government was compelled to adopt minor measures in the right direction to end its complicity,” Barghouti said.

“But it’s way short of the UK’s legal obligations to end complicity in genocide, in apartheid, in illegal occupation. So, we must work further to grow our BDS movement.”

The motion puts additional pressure on the government to take a stronger stance against Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Last week, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced a ban on importing goods from Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law. Addressing Parliament, Miliband denounced “settler terrorists” for carrying out what he described as “ethnic cleansing” in parts of the West Bank.

However, the foreign secretary said he “wholeheartedly” opposes BDS, stressing that the UK would continue to “support important and valued trade” with Israel that adheres to international law.

Peter Leary, deputy director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, told Al Jazeera that Wednesday’s vote marked a “tipping point”.

“In marked contrast to Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s attempt to dismiss the Palestinian BDS movement, trade unions are paving the way to secure real change, and we must keep up the pressure to force the government to take meaningful action and end all military, diplomatic and economic support for Israel,” he said.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the Trades Union Congress and the UK government but did not receive a response at the time of publication.

articles.title: Syria's parliament votes to scrap Assad-era terrorism court, nullify rulings
articles.summary: Middle East News: Syria's parliament voted on Wednesday to abolish a counter-terrorism court established during the reign of former President Bashar al-Assad and nullif.
articles.body: Syria's parliament voted on Wednesday to abolish a counter-terrorism court established during the reign of former President Bashar al-Assad and nullify the legal effects of its rulings.The counter-terrorism court was set up in 2012 in an effort to crush an uprising against Assad's rule, and was reportedly used to prosecute thousands of anti-Assad Syrians on terrorism-related charges.Wednesday's decision formalises the court's abolition, after Syria's new authorities had already been treating it as defunct.In June 2025, President Ahmed al-Sharaa issued a decree dismissing 67 judges who had served on what he then described as the "abolished Counter-Terrorism Court". Syria's constitutional declaration of March 2025 had also called for undoing the effects of what it termed unjust rulings handed down by the court, including the return of confiscated property.In 2024, the United Nations Human Rights Committee said the 2012 law that created the court had failed to provide adequate judicial guarantees, and it raised concerns over arbitrary detention, torture or ill-treatment, as well as the court's independence. The committee also noted that the court had been permitted to depart from standard procedures during prosecutions and trials.Separately, the UN's international, impartial and independent mechanism said in a 2024 report that the counter-terrorism court had formed part of the judicial system through which people held by Assad-era security agencies could be prosecuted. The report documented widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment throughout the government's detention system.According to Reuters, Wednesday's vote took place during the opening weeks of the first parliament to be formed since Assad's removal from power on December 8 2024.Assad was removed from power when an 11-day offensive by opposition forces led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) captured Damascus and forced him to flee to Russia.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
